query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary/ternary subsets, variations in mechanical properties stem from differences in intrinsic stacking fault energy (SFE) and associated local bonding heterogeneity, which modify dislocation dissociation (and hence mobility) and solid solution strengthening. These changes are driven by alterations in the atomic size mismatch and bonding interaction when one or more constituents are removed, thereby tuning the balance between work hardening and failure behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Single‐phase FCC high-entropy alloys based on equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its lower constituent (quaternary and ternary) subsets obtained via thermomechanical processing.
generation.intervention: Design and fabricate a series of FCC alloys where one or two constituents are systematically removed from the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline while keeping processing parameters constant.
generation.conditions: All alloys are processed (thermomechanically and heat treated) under identical conditions, and mechanical tests (e.g., micropillar compression, nanoindentation) are conducted at room temperature and cryogenic conditions to assess temperature-dependent effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Variations in stacking fault energy and dislocation core structure (as mediated by differences in atomic size mismatch and local bonding heterogeneity).
generation.mechanism: Substitution of one or more elements alters the average atomic size and electronic bonding environment, which changes the stacking fault energy. A lower SFE increases the dissociation distance of dislocations into Shockley partials, thus impeding dislocation motion and modifying work hardening. Conversely, an SFE closer to that of the equiatomic baseline may lower the barriers to dislocation glide, resulting in diminished strength. This dislocation-mediated mechanism underpins the observed variations in deformation and failure behaviors among these alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the equiatomic quinary baseline, subsets with altered compositions will exhibit measurable differences in dislocation splitting distances (indicating a change in SFE), critical resolved shear stresses, and work-hardening rates. For instance, alloys with a lower SFE are predicted to show higher yield strength and enhanced work hardening due to more robust dislocation interactions, though these effects may trade off with ductility. The magnitude of these differences will be on the order of tens of MPa variations in CRSS and several nanometers change in partial dislocation separations, within the limits observed in similar FCC HEA studies.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy processed into a single-phase FCC structure with a known CRSS (e.g., ~33–43 MPa as seen in similar HEAs) and established dislocation characteristics (partial separation distances of roughly 3.5–8 nm as measured in comparable materials).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to FCC single-phase high-entropy alloys (or near-equiatomic alloys) produced by comparable thermomechanical methods, and may not extend to alloys that either fall outside the single-phase region or whose deformation is dominated by phase transformations or other mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative predictions of yield stress and dislocation separation rely on the assumption that the primary effect of constituent reduction is to adjust the SFE and atomic misfit; however, other factors (such as residual microsegregation, secondary phase precipitations, and processing history) may also impact the mechanical outcome. The precise size of the changes is therefore uncertain and should be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a systematic series of FCC single-phase alloys ranging from the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni to selected quaternary and ternary variants, ensuring identical processing conditions. Use high-resolution electron microscopy and in situ mechanical testing (e.g., micropillar compression) to measure dislocation structures (splitting distances) and determine the critical resolved shear stress under identical loading conditions.
measurements: Dislocation core structure and separation distances (as a proxy for stacking fault energy)
Residual stresses/microstructural uniformity by EBSD or TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the removal of constituents (altering atomic size mismatch and bonding) does not yield statistically significant differences in measured stacking fault energies, dislocation dissociation distances, and corresponding mechanical properties (CRSS, yield stress) compared to the equiatomic baseline, then the hypothesis that SFE-related mechanisms govern the observed mechanical-property differences would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Size effect, critical resolved shear stress, stacking fault energy, and solid solution strengthening in the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprise a novel class of scientifically and technologically interesting materials. Among these, equatomic CrMnFeCoNi with the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure is noteworthy because its ductility and strength increase with decreasing temperature while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures. Here we report for the first time by single-crystal micropillar compression that its bulk room temperature critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) is ~33–43 MPa, ~10 times higher than that of pure nickel. CRSS depends on pillar size with an inverse power-law scaling exponent of –0.63 independent of orientation. Planar ½ < 110 > {111} dislocations dissociate into Shockley partials whose separations range from ~3.5–4.5 nm near the screw orientation to ~5–8 nm near the edge, yielding a stacking fault energy of 30 ± 5 mJ/m2.
